title: Evaluating Statistical Claims, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with statistical claims, and then a two-question checklist that settles almost every study.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it's so tempting.
Trap one. A survey found that people who garden report less stress. Students conclude that gardening reduces stress.
People chose whether to garden, so the study is observational. It supports only an association between gardening and lower stress.
beats.right: gardening is associated with less stress

beats.say: Trap two. A random sample of one university's students tells you about that university's students. Students extend it to all adults.
A result applies to the group the sample was randomly drawn from. Here, that means the students at that university.
Trap three. Thousands of call-in votes to a radio show are still a self-selected group. Students trust the large number.
A large sample doesn't cure bias. Only random selection from the population makes a sample representative.
Trap four. Random selection and random assignment answer different questions. A study with random selection but no assignment can't claim cause.
Random selection is about who is studied, and lets you generalize. Random assignment is about who gets which treatment, and lets you claim cause.
Trap five. If a question asks by how many percentage points two groups differ, you subtract the percents. Students divide them instead.
Subtract the percents. Sixty-five percent minus forty-five percent is twenty percentage points.
Desmos is no help here, because this skill is about reasoning, not computing. The fast way is a two-question checklist, used on every study.
Question one. Who was selected, and how? If they were selected randomly from a population, the conclusion can apply to that population. Otherwise, it applies only to the participants.
Question two. Were treatments randomly assigned? If yes, causal words such as causes, leads to, or is effective are allowed. If no, only is associated with.

card.sub: Yes: cause allowed. No: association only.

beats.say: Then eliminate any answer that claims more than both checks allow. The most modest correct claim is usually the answer.

card.text: Eliminate answers that claim too much

beats.say: Now a practice problem. Researchers randomly selected one thousand adults in a state, and found that those who drink coffee daily reported better focus. Does the study show that coffee improves focus? Pause the video, try it, and then watch the answer.

card.sub: Coffee drinkers report better focus. Cause?

beats.say: Question one. Participants were randomly selected, so the result can be generalized to adults in that state.
Question two. Treatments weren't assigned. People chose whether to drink coffee. So the study can only show an association, and can't show that coffee improves focus.
The best conclusion is that, among adults in the state, daily coffee drinking is associated with better focus. The study doesn't show that coffee causes the improvement.
One more skill. In an experiment, twenty-two of forty people in one group improved, and fourteen of forty in the other. By how many percentage points do the rates differ?
Twenty-two out of forty is fifty-five percent, and fourteen out of forty is thirty-five percent.
Fifty-five minus thirty-five is twenty. So the rates differ by twenty percentage points.
To recap. Without random assignment, claim only an association. Without random selection, don't generalize beyond the participants.
beats.item: No assignment: association. No selection: participants only.

beats.say: A large sample doesn't cure bias, and a difference between percents is reported in percentage points.
beats.item: Size is not bias; subtract percents

beats.say: That completes Problem-Solving and Data Analysis. In the next unit, we study Geometry and Trigonometry, starting with area and volume.
